03d23adb-52fc-5e9a-b84a-0cf1c00fe196.name: Seljuqs (Great Seljuqs)
03d23adb-52fc-5e9a-b84a-0cf1c00fe196.history:
Seljuq Bey, who laid the foundations for the Great Seljuq state, was the son of Duqaq Subashi, a commander of the state of Oghuz \[Oğuz\] near the Caspian Sea. On the death of his father, Seljuq Bey became *subashi* at a very young age and increased his power very quickly. To resolve conflicts with the sultan of the state of Oghuz, he surrounded himself with Oghuz Turks and settled at Jend near the Oxus River in AH 375 / AD 985 and converted to Islam.  
Seljuq Bey allied himself to the Samanids and established himself at Nur near Bukhara, to defend the northern frontiers. He was succeeded by his son Arslan Bey. After the fall of the Samanids at the hands of the Karakhanids in 399 / 999, the good relationship the Seljuqs had enjoyed with the Karakhanids and the Ghaznavids came to an end.  
The capture and imprisonment of Arslan Bey by the Ghaznavids in 416 / 1025 caused a split in the Seljuqs. Arslan Bey was succeeded by his nephews Tuğrul \[Tughril\] and Çağrı \[Chaghrı\]. Having defeated the Ghaznawids at Serahs (429 / 1038) and Dandanakan (431 / 1040), they founded the Great Seljuq state. Tuğrul Bey proclaimed himself sultan. Nishapur was briefly capital of the state, before being replaced by Marw.  
The Great Seljuq state, founded in the territory of present-day Iran, saw its power increase significantly between 431 and 485 (1040–92), the years of the 'first imperial age'. Under the reigns of Alparslan \[Alp Arslan\] and Melikşah \[Malik Shah\], who succeeded Tuğrul Bey, the Seljuqs extended their dominion towards Anatolia, the Middle East and Central Asia.  
After the death of Sultan Melikşah in 485 / 1092, disputes over succession, the Batini rebellions, the Turcoman revolts and the Mongol invasions caused the fragmentation of the Great Seljuqs into four states (the Seljuqs of Iraq, Syria, Kirman and Anatolia \[Rum\]) and the emergence of numerous *atabegs* \[commanders\]. In spite of the efforts of Sultan Sanjar, who came to power in 510 / 1117, to confederate the states, the Battle of Qatawan \[Katvan\] fought against the Karakhitais in 536 / 1141 and the Oghuz rebellions of 548 / 1153 paved the road to an inevitable end. The Great Seljuq state officially ceased to exist with the death of Sultan Sanjar in 552 / 1157.

0a03f889-edff-5b28-a555-d7350135e797.name: Deccan Sultanate
0a03f889-edff-5b28-a555-d7350135e797.history:
The Deccan denotes the region in southern India that was witness to a group of rulers, both local and from distant lands, who travelled to the area and founded empires there. They included soldiers, ministers, sufis, craftsmen and artists. Over time, the governors of this region broke away from the Bahmani dynasty to form five dynasties that ruled different parts of the region.  
  
The first of these was the Imad Shahi Sultans of Berar, located in the far north. Their capital was in Elichpur, which was situated on the north-western plateau. Then there were the Nizam Shahi Sultans of Ahmednagar. A third and important dynasty that lay toward the east was the Qutb Shahi realm of Golconda, and to the west ruled the Adil Shahi sons of Bijapur. Located at the very centre of the plateau was the former Bahmani capital of Bidar, where the Barid Shahi Sultans reigned.  
  
The Deccan was well placed geographically for long-distance Indian Ocean trade routes. It came to be identified mainly with the regions of Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Goa.  
  
In the 14th and 18th centuries, Islam was the most followed religion in the region. A Muslim sultanate had been established in Delhi (northern India) toward the beginning of the 13th century. Between 1323 and 1340, the Deccan was ruled by three main dynasties: the Marathi-speaking Yadavas, the Kannada-speaking Hoysala and the Telugu-speaking Kakatiyas.  
  
Firuz Shah Tughlaq was a ruler of the Tughluq dynasty and ruled the Sultanate of Delhi from 1351 to 1388. He started recruiting Persian-speaking men of letters, administrators, artisans and soldiers. In 1354, Firuz also commenced the building of his new capital, Firuzabad, 27 kilometres south of Gulbarga. Before the reign of the Firuz Shah Tughlaq, two new dynasties were established in the Deccan, namely, the Sangamas at Vijayanagara in the southern Deccan (1336) and the Bahmanis at Gulbarga in the north (1347). This gave rise to the renowned Indo-Islamic culture in the Deccan. However, when Amir Timur sacked Delhi in 1399, the Tughluqs had to withdraw to their chosen capital, Firuzabad.  
  
In 1422, Sultan Ahmad Bahmani was succeeded by his brother, Firuz, who transferred the state’s capital from Gulbarga to Bidar, located in the heart of the Deccan plateau. While Delhi was sacked, Bidar was the new and impressive imperial city. It was known for its architecture, which was inspired by Timurid Samarqand. Between the 14th and 18th centuries, the Deccan plateau witnessed an efflorescence of art and architecture. The rulers commissioned monumental architecture using materials such as bronze, silver, stone, glass and lacquer. They also commissioned textiles made of cotton and silk.  
  
The monument that resembled Timurid architecture the most was the madrasa of Mahmud Gawan (1418). Gawan was a cosmopolitan Iranian, having travelled to Anatolia, Syria, Egypt and central Asia. He reached the Bahmani capital, and after being interviewed by Sultan Ahmad II Bahmani, he was made an emir with a command of 1,000 cavalrymen. In 1499, he was also made regent for two monarchs.  
  
Muslims who came from Iran and central Asia to south Asia brought a cosmopolitan Persian culture with them. By the 15th century, Iran and central Asia were ruled by the Timurids and Turkmen. During this time there was cultural exchange with the Deccan Sultanates. In the southern kingdom of Vijayanagara, Turkic mercenaries were being recruited, and this gave rise to a ruling class that took to Persianate ideas and practices. Commerce and military concerns also allied Vijayanagara with the Persianate world.  
  
In the 16th century, there were changes that occurred in the political climate of Iran and central Asia. The Timurid empire disintegrated after being attacked by the Safavids and Shaybanids descended from Chengiz Khan. There were Timurids who, as a consequence of these attacks, moved to northern India, and this relocation marked the beginning of the Mughal Empire (1526–1858).  
  
The Bahmani state divided into smaller kingdoms: Berar, Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Bidar and Golconda. Along with Vijayanagara, the five states of the Deccan Sultanates vied with each other for land and resources. These states had a great number of foreigners, including Africans, who were recruited as military slaves, as well as Arabs, Iranians and central Asians. The Nizam Shahis of Ahmadnagar, the Qutb Shahs of Golconda and the Adil Shahis of Bijapur, known for its syncretic religious policy, all had ties with the Safavid court.  
  
By 1565, the joint armies of Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda dealt a severe blow to Vijayanagara, which had already been reduced geographically and consequently lost any influence in the region. As a result, Berar and Bidar became a part of Ahmadnagar (1574) and Bijapur (1619), respectively. In 1636, a treaty was signed according to which Ahmadnagar was divided between the Mughal Empire and Bijapur. In the same year, Bijapur and Golconda accepted Mughal suzerainty, and half a century later they were incorporated into the Mughal Empire.

• Michell, George, Architecture and Art of the Deccan Sultanates, UK: Cambridge University Press, 1999.  
• Parodi, Laura and Eaton, Richard, The Visual World of Muslim India. I.B. Tauris, London (2014).

0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.name: Alawids
0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.area: Morocco. Capitals: Fez, Meknes and Rabat
0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.history:
The greatness of the Sa'dids was disproportionately linked to exceptionally favourable circumstances and the personalities of two sovereigns: 'Abd al-Malik and Ahmad al-Mansur.  
On the death of the latter (AH 1011 / AD 1603), the political and economic difficulties resurfaced, as did the unrest of the brotherhoods and the piracy that reinforced the breakdown of relations with Europe.  
The Alawid Sharifs, who held some power in Tafilalet, used their religious power and their skill as warriors and organisers to take control of eastern Morocco before taking Fez (1076 / 1666) and then Marrakesh (1079 / 1669).  
Mulay Isma'il, the most renowned of the sultans (1082–1139 / 1672–1727), consolidated the work of the founders of the dynasty and breathed new life into Moroccan civilisation. He fought the Turks and took the places still held by the Europeans on the Atlantic. However, this military power proved to be too costly and, after the death of Mulay Isma'il, Morocco fell into a deep political and economic crisis, which worsened the effect of the loss of revenues generated through privateering.  
After 30 years of chaos, Morocco experienced a spectacular recovery under Sidi Muhammad bin 'Abdallah (1170–1204 1757–90), who regained control of the army and the tribal administration and opened the country to the Atlantic by developing Tangiers and Casablanca and founding Essaouira, as well as re-establishing diplomatic and commercial links with Europe and even setting up relations with the USA. This recovery was cut short by a plague epidemic and a great famine, with the population plunging from five to three million between 1189 and 1214 / 1776 and 1800. The country became inward-looking and its weakness left it wide open to the vast European colonial movement.

12372d12-9b12-553c-861f-285f6d090ef6.name: Zirids
12372d12-9b12-553c-861f-285f6d090ef6.history:
The Fatimid Amir al-Mu'izz Ibn Badis al-Ziri, the new governor of Cairo, entrusted the Emirate of Ifriqiya \[Tunisia\] in AH 362 / AD 973, to one of his faithful lieutenants, the dignitary Yusuf ibn Ziri al-Sanhagi, advising him to adopt a policy of benevolence towards the towns and their inhabitants.  
Thus a dynasty was born that, at its peak, reigned over a vast area that stretched to central Maghreb. The Zirids had two administrative towns, Kairouan and then Mahdia, before returning to Monastir for their eternal rest. Under the Zirids, and in particular during the reign of al-Mu'izz (406–53 / 1016–62), Ifriqiya was a prosperous land, a fact recorded by many chroniclers. However, an event fraught with consequences jeopardised Zirid power and marked the history of medieval Ifriqiya: the Hilalian invasion launched in 443 / 1052 by the Caliph of Cairo to punish his vassal al-Mu'izz for having rejected the suzerainty of the Fatimids over his kingdom. The Zirids lost control of the country and withdrew to Mahdia, from where they were expelled in 542 / 1148 when the town was taken by the Normans.  
The Zirids made an important contribution to Ifriqiyan art, in particular:  
• The repair and decoration of the Great Mosque of Tunis, including the dome erected in 380 / 991 over the entrance of the prayer room, which brings together the most significant decorative elements of the time.  
• Decorative work on the Great Mosque of Kairouan, such as the painted ceilings and the addition of a *minbar* (pulpit) with high-quality wood carvings of plant motifs.  
• Expansions and conversions of other holy sites in places such as Monastir, Sousse and Sfax.  
• The construction of princely residences in the royal Fatimid city of Sabra al-Mansuriya at the gateway to Kairouan.  
• Fortifications in several of the county's coastal towns such as Monastir, where they are thought to be responsible for the al-Sayyida *ribat* (fortress), which was also their necropolis.

1b44d492-30f4-535f-900d-c5ef2637794f.name: Seljuqs (Anatolian)
1b44d492-30f4-535f-900d-c5ef2637794f.also_known_as: The Seljuqs of Rum or Rum-Seljuqs
1b44d492-30f4-535f-900d-c5ef2637794f.area: Anatolia (also known as Asia Minor, the Asian part of modern Turkey)
1b44d492-30f4-535f-900d-c5ef2637794f.history:
From the early AH 5th / AD 11th century, the Oghuz \[Oğuz\] Turks began making incursions into Anatolia and, following the battle of Manzikert (Malazgirt, in eastern Turkey) between the Great Seljuqs and the Byzantines in 463 / 1071, the Great Seljuq Sultan Alparslan \[Alp Arslan\] sent several Turcoman leaders and chiefs to take Anatolia. The first Turkish emirates were soon established in Anatolia: the Saltuqids in Erzurum, the Mengüjekids in Erzincan and the Danishmendids in Sivas.  
Süleyman Shah, who took Konya and the surrounding area, founded the Anatolian Seljuq state in 469 / 1077. Konya was briefly the capital, before being replaced by Iznik after it was taken by the Seljuqs in 472 / 1080. With the advent of the First Crusade in 489 / 1096, Iznik and the region returned to Byzantine rule and the Seljuqs re-established their capital at Konya.  
Having reigned solely over Konya and the surrounding area, the Seljuqs of Anatolia quickly expanded their territory. In the 7th/13th century, by installing lesser rulers in newly conquered regions, they came to control much of Anatolia, with the exception of the coastal regions of the west.  
The Anatolian Seljuq state had its political, economic and cultural heyday during the reign of Alaeddin Keykubad I \['Ala' al-Din Kay Qubadh\], 616–34/ 1220–37. The conquest of Alanya on the Mediterranean coast elevated the Seljuqs to the status of great power on the maritime trading routes, while the caravan routes that criss-crossed Anatolia enabled them to increase their power by taxing the movement of goods.  
The unification of Turkey was consolidated and public safety was assured in Anatolia. Starting with Konya, Kayseri and Sivas, the citadels of many Anatolian towns were fortified, and the towns themselves modernised and endowed with monuments. The Anatolian Seljuq state began to decline after the Babai rebellions during the reign of Gıyaseddin Keyhüsrev II \[Giyath al-Din Kay Khusraw, 634–44 / 1237–46) in 640 / 1242 and defeat to the Mongols at the Battle of Kösedag \[Köse Dagh\] in 641 / 1243. After that, Anatolia was governed by the Mongols. The death of Sultan Gıyaseddin Mesud III \[Giyath al-Din Masud\] in 708 / 1308 marked the official end of the Seljuq State.

1d206364-a251-5fda-81dc-54a09e646e5e.name: Aghlabids
1d206364-a251-5fda-81dc-54a09e646e5e.history:
The spread of the Abbasid Empire and the re-establishment of the Umayyads in Al-Andalus and the Idrisids in Morocco, led the Abbasids to establish a local principality in North Africa to protect themselves against these rival powers surrounding their kingdom. In AH 184 / AD 800, Caliph Harun al-Rashid (169–93 / 786–809) gave Ifriqiya (Tunisia) to Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab (184–6 / 800–11), as a hereditary principality for him and his descendants to rule.  
Despite the many revolts they faced in their early days, the Aghlabids managed to establish their rule over Ifriqiya, pacifying the country and developing trade and communication. They rebuilt cities and villages, and constructed a series of fortresses along the Tunisian coast to defend the country from attack from their rivals or from the Byzantines.  
The Aghlabids controlled most of the islands in the western Mediterranean, including Sicily and Malta, and their influence extended as far as southern Italy. Ifriqiya experienced great prosperity under the Aghlabids, evident in the wealth of their architectural legacy, which included the Great Mosque of Kairouan and nearby reservoirs, and the Mosque of Zaytuna. Agriculture, weaving and ceramics also prospered, making Ifriqiya the main trade link between the Middle East and North Africa, and between Al-Andalus and Sudan.  
The inevitable fall of the Aghlabids came about mainly because of the brutality of the ruling prince Ibrahim II and the atmosphere of frivolity and profligacy that pervaded the reign of Ziyadat Allah III (290–6 / 903–9), which led the people of Ifriqiya to reject the Aghlabids and to refuse to support them against the spread of Shi'ism. Ifriqiya fell without a fight in 296 / 909 to the armies of Abu 'Abdallah al-Sana'ani, the founder of the Fatimid Dynasty, which went on to rule Egypt, Syria and Palestine.

26e98384-aec9-54a7-8d11-2fa3e84a1d52.name: Umayyads of al-Andalus
26e98384-aec9-54a7-8d11-2fa3e84a1d52.area: Iberian peninsula, excepting Christian kingdoms of the north
26e98384-aec9-54a7-8d11-2fa3e84a1d52.history: 'Abd al-Rahman bin Hisham, grandson of the last Umayyad caliph of Damascus and survivor of his family's massacre at the hands of the Abbasids, arrived in Córdoba in AH 132 / AD 750. He founded a dynasty that broke off his allegiance with the Abbasid caliphate of Baghdad and governed al-Andalus from AH 138 to 422 / AD 756 to 1031, initially as an emirate and then, in AH 316 / AD 929, as a full caliphate ('Abd al-Rahman III). A pacific and hugely rich state, the Caliphate of Córdoba ruled the whole of al-Andalus and nurtured a brilliant civilisation that rivalled that of Baghdad and eclipsed those in the Christian West.

275fd924-3ed6-5493-ba0f-732cc27640a1.name: Timurids
275fd924-3ed6-5493-ba0f-732cc27640a1.area: Central Asia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Anatolia [Turkey] and India
275fd924-3ed6-5493-ba0f-732cc27640a1.history:
The Timurid Empire was founded by Tamerlane (Timur the Lame), the son of Turagay \[Taraghay\], the *bey* of the Barlas, a vassal tribe of the Chaghatays in Turkistan. Timur succeeded his father (d. AH 761 / AD 1360) and his uncle (d. 762 / 1361) as the leader of the Barlas. He increased his power in a short time and was proclaimed the 'amir' of the Chaghatay state. He founded the Timurid state, making Samarkand his capital.  
In a short time, Tamerlane conquered a vast region encompassing Azerbaijan, Khwarazm, Khurasan, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Anatolia, India and many other lands, and stretching from India to Damascus, from the Gulf of Basra to the Lake Aral and Anatolia.  
Tamerlane defeated the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I ('Thunderbolt') at the Battle of Ankara in 804 / 1402 and struck a deadly blow against the Ottomans. Tamerlane died in 807 / 1405 on an expedition to China.  
The contest for the throne following Tamerlane's death shook his empire greatly. Shah Rukh (r. 811–50 / 1409–47) moved his capital to Herat, leaving his son Uluğ Bey \[Ulugh Beg\], a renowned astronomer, in Samarkand. In this period Samarkand and Herat were furbished with magnificent monuments and became centres of arts and sciences. Uluğ Bey succeeded his father but was assassinated in 910 / 1449. This led to a great conflict, which finally ended in 854 / 1451 when Abu Sa'id ascended the throne. The Timurid Empire reached its zenith during his reign and the reign of his son Hüseyin Baykara. The Timurid Empire fell to the in 910 / 1505.  
Timurids constructed many monuments in cities such as Samarkand, Herat, Bukhara, Mashhad, Tabriz, Balkh and Yazd. The complexes of Uluğ Bey in Samarkand and Bukhara, the Gök Masjid in Tabriz, the mausoleum group of Shah Zinda in Samarkand, the complex of Hodja Ahmed Yasawi in Yesi and Bibi Hatun Mosque at Samarkand are among the most noteworthy monuments of the period.

29eaeead-971d-5ced-a2f3-a650a47f04ff.name: Safavids
29eaeead-971d-5ced-a2f3-a650a47f04ff.history:
The Safavid dynasty of Turkic origin was founded by the religious leader Safi al-Din Ardabili, who lived in Ardabil from 659 to 754 / 1252 to 1334. His religious order spread quickly in Anatolia, Iran and Iraq. The dynasty was supported by Tamerlane, the Ottomans and the Aq Qoyunlus and became more powerful especially during the reign of Hodja Ali, a grandson of Ardabili. When Shaykh Junayd, a grandson of Hodja Ali, interfered with the internal affairs of the Mamluks and the Qara Qoyunlus, relations with these powers deteriorated. Around the end of the AH 9th / AD 15th century, their relations with the Aq Qoyunlus also deteriorated and this led to the dissolution of the dynasty. However, the Safavids recovered quickly and Shah Isma'il established the Safavid State in 906 / 1501, with Tabriz as the capital.  
Joining forces with the Shi'a, the Safavids ruled over a vast area encompassing Iran, Iraq, Caucasia and east Anatolia. The Ottoman Sultan Selim I defeated Shah Isma'il at Çaldıran in 920 / 1514. Shah Isma'il was succeeded by his son Shah Tahmasp in 930 / 1524 and the capital was moved to Qazwin. After Shah Tahmasp, the Safavid State was ruled by Isma'il Mirza, Hamza Mirza, Shah Abbas, Sam Mirza, Abbas II, Shah Sulayman I, Shah Husayn, Tahmasp II and finally by Abbas III. Nadir Shah of Afshar origin brought the Safavid State to an end in 1150 / 1737 by conquering Iran.  
The Safavids built numerous monuments during their rule of approximately 250 years, especially in Iran. The palaces of Jihil Sütun and Hasht Bahisht, the Kiosk of Ali Kapı and the mosques of Masjid-i Shah and Shaykh Lutf Allah in Isfahan are among the major monuments of this period.

2c8ab4b0-e8bd-5ae8-982b-758f178293e4.name: Aq Qoyunlu
2c8ab4b0-e8bd-5ae8-982b-758f178293e4.area: Eastern Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran, Iraq
2c8ab4b0-e8bd-5ae8-982b-758f178293e4.history:
The Aq Qoyunlu (meaning “white sheep”) were a confederation of Turkmen nomads centered in Diyar Bakr in power from Hegira 780/AD 1378 to Hegira 908/AD 1508. They came to power in the late 14th century AD and served under Timur (AD 1370–1405). Under the leader Uzun Hasan (AD 1457–1478) they went on to rule a territory stretching from eastern Anatolia (AD 1378–1503) to western Iran Khurasan, as well as Iraq and the Persian Gulf. Ultimately, they were defeated by the Ottomans and the Safavids.  
  
The first Aq Qoyunlu leader was Tur-Ali (b. Pahlavan), in power in the decade of Hegira 740–50/AD 1339–49 during a time of armed clashes with forces from Trebizond. To regain peace, in Hegira 753/AD 1352, Tur-Ali’s son Fakr-al-din Qutlu was married to the sister of Trebizond’s ruler Alexios III (AD 1349–90). Trebizond was safe from Aq Qoyunlu’s attacks until it fell to the Ottomans in Hegira 865/AD 1461. Tur-Ali died sometime between Hegira 753/AD 1352 and Hegira 764/AD 1363 and his successor Qutlu died in Hegira 791/AD 1389. Leadership was passed on to Qutlu’s son Ahmad, who was later replaced by his brother Qara Yoluz (or Yülük) Otman Beg, or Qara Otman.  
  
Qara Otman joined the ruler Timur in Hegira 802/AD1399–1400, and participated in his campaigns in Sivas and the battle of Ankara (Hegira 804/AD 1402). In return, Timur made Qara Otman an amir and an official leader of the Aq Qoyunlu tribe. The confederation of the Aq Qoyunlu also acquired the fortress city of Amed (Diyar Bakr), which would continue to be their capital for seventy years.  
  
By the time of Qara Otman’s death in Hegira 839/AD 1435, the Aq Qoyunlu, allied with the Timurids, had become an unquestioned authority in the region of Armenia and Diyar Bakr. Qara Otman had chosen Ali as his heir, however this new successor was not able to retain power in the face of his male relatives and renounced his position of leadership in Hegira 841/AD 1438–39 and went into self-imposed exile in Egypt. Ali’s brother Hamza was a powerful leader of the Aq Qoyunlu for a time, until his death in Hegira 848/AD 1444.  
  
It was Uzun Hasan (Long Hasan) under whose rule the Aq Qoyunlu were reunified and gained strength. In Hegira 862/AD 1458, he raided Georgia and came to be known as ghazi (“fighter for the faith”), and renewed the Aq Qoyulu’s friendship with the house of Trebizond. He also married the Komnenian princess Theodora, forming an alliance that grew in strength in the face of threat from the Ottomans. However, the Ottomans were superior in weaponry and strength. Due to this military imbalance, Uzun Hasan refrained from going to war with them. In the summer of Hegira 873/AD 1468, Uzun Hasan defeated the Qara Qoyunlu and conquered Azerbaijan.  
  
The Timurid ruler Abu Sa’id had been ruling Herat since Hegira 855/AD 1451 when he was taken prisoner and put to death by Uzun Hasan. Now that his adversaries had been eliminated, Uzun Hasan marched to western Iran and annexed the Iranian provinces up to Khorasan and transferred his government to Tabriz. However, he failed to assert his rule over the Timurids of Khorasan. In late Hegira 875/early AD 1471, Uzun Hasan moved his garrison from Khorasan to the western frontier, which led to friendly relations between Tabriz and Herat. However, in Qaraman his interests conflicted with those of the Ottomans and Mamluks.  
  
Uzun Hasan died on the eve of Sawwal, Hegira 882/AD 5–6 January 1478. Before his death he reacted to the defiance of his son Ogurlu Mohammad by designating Ogurlu’s brother Kalil as his heir. However, Kalil was soon killed in Rabiʿa II, Hegira 883/AD July 1478 in an armed struggle with his fourteen-year-old brother Ya’qub and his supporters, near Koy. Ya’qub came to power and his reign lasted for a period of twelve years. He died mysteriously on I1 Safar AH 896/AD 24 December 1491. During his reign he had convinced Kalil’s supporters to come to his side. However, Ya’qub had no interest in the religious sentiments of the masses and their practices, alienating large groups of his followers, particularly the Turkmans. As a consequence of Ya’qub’s death, the Aq Qoyunlu were engaged in constant power struggles.  
  
Ya’qub’s eight-year-old son Baysongor was crowned in Hegira 896/AD 1491 under the guidance of Ṣufi Kalil Beg Mawsellu. However, he was expelled from Tabriz in Rajab, Hegira 897/AD May 1492 by his cousin Rostam (descended from Maqṣūd, descendent of Uzun Ḥasan), who was supported by the Pornak and Qajar tribes. Baysongor was killed in Hegira 898/AD 1493. Rostam attempted to create a reconciliation between the religious establishment and the popular Sufi orders.  
  
In Hegira 902/AD 1497, Rostam was ousted by his cousin Govde (“dwarf”) Aḥmad (b. Ogurlu Moḥammad), who had returned from his exile in Ottoman territory. Ahmad’s politics brought about a revolt by the amirs, who defeated and killed him on Rabīʿa II, Hegira 903/AD December 1497. With Ahmad’s death, the Aq Qoyunlu empire further disintegrated. The last Aq Qoyunlu sultan was Morad (b. Yaʿqub), who took help from Ottoman troops to gain the throne, but he was defeated and killed by Esma’il Qizilbash’s troops. The last of the surviving Aq Qoyunlu tribes were then absorbed into other groups, such as the Qizilbash.

2cf9d6c6-0226-5c5d-8710-c052cc2ac4c7.name: Al-Busaid
2cf9d6c6-0226-5c5d-8710-c052cc2ac4c7.history:
The Al Busaid dynasty, also known as the House of Al Said, was a line of rulers that included the Sultanate of Oman (1744-1856), the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman (1856-1970) and the Sultanate of Zanzibar (1856-1964). Founded by Ahmad bin Said al- Busaidi, ruler of Oman and the east African territories, the Al Busaid dynasty governed the region for 250 years. During Ahmad bin Said al- Busaidi’s 39-year reign, the Omani navy was a formidable presence in the Indian Ocean, second only to the British navy. It very easily expelled the Persian forces from the region while protecting Ottoman ships in the Gulf of Oman and the Indian Ocean.  
  
The modern history of Oman has witnessed two different systems of governance: the *imama* system and the sultanate system. An *imamah* (imamate) can refer to the office of the imam or to his spiritual leadership. Imams are spiritual leaders who may exercise control over a particular region. To receive the *imamah*, a ruler has to be elected.  
  
Imam Ahmed ibn Said (1741-1783) established the sultanate system during his rule. It was the first time that a separation was established between the two political systems. He saved Oman from a civil war, restored it to its regional place in the Afro-Asian and maritime system and made a decisive contribution to the shaping of Oman’s modern history - a history of the sultanate as opposed to the *imama* system. In 1741, he received the *imamah*. Ahmed was remarkable for his firm attitude towards colonial hegemony. This became apparent when he barred the East India Company from setting up a branch in Muscat. The long reign of Ahmed ibn Said (about 39 years) also witnessed changes and new tendencies in Omani society. His reign not only forged a new vision of a political system but also helped lay the foundation of a new political, national and cultural identity.  
  
Ahmed ibn Said died in 1778 and was succeeded by his son, Said bin Ahmed, a pious leader who divided duties among palace officials along religious, administrative and military lines. Said bin Ahmed kept his *imamah* and moved to al-Rustaq, where he remained until his death in 1811. In 1783, his son, Hamad bin Said, decided to move his court to the coastal city of Muscat and make the city his political capital. He also took the title of sultan, signalling his power.  
  
Hamad bin Said was a capable ruler who did much for the country in his eight-year reign. He facilitated reform policy in the initial stages of the transition but died suddenly in 1792. On his death, Oman’s political system was divided into three main parts: Said bin Ahmed, the official imam, stayed in al-Rustaq; Sayyid Sultan bin Ahmed (who succeeded Hamad ibn Said) retained Muscat as his base of power; and finally, Sayf, Ahmed ibn Sa’id’s third son, took the city of Sohar (located near Hormuz) as his centre of power. Thus in 1793, and with the collaboration of the British, the Islamic state of Oman, which had been a unified nation, was now fragmented into three separate polities.  
  
After his accession to the throne in 1792, Sayyid Sultan ibn Ahmed (1792-1804) used his power and intellect to restore Muscat to the place it was under the rule of his father Ahmed. Oman became an ally of France in the region east of Africa and the Indian Ocean, especially as Britain was beginning to appear a hazard to Oman, India and all the countries of the Gulf.  
  
Sayyid Said bin Sultan, aged 17, came to power in 1806 on his father’s death and remained ruler for half a century until his death in 1856. He was the first sayyid of Oman, received the title of sultan and was also called ‘the Great’. Oman was established as a major commercial and maritime power in the Indian Ocean during his reign. He was succeeded by Thuwaini bin Said al-Said, who was the third son of Said bin Sultan and ruled from 1856-1866.  
  
Between 1866 and 1970, Oman experienced the reign of six other rulers. Finally, from 1970 to 2020, Oman was ruled by Sultan Qaboos, who modernized the region. The current heir to the throne since 2020 is Sultan Haitham bin Tariq.  
  
Bibliography  
• Ghubash, Hussein, Oman - The Islamic Democratic Tradition, London and New York: Routledge, 2006.  
• Jones, Jeremy and Ridout, Nicholas, A History of Modern Oman, Cambridge (UK) and New York: Cambridge University Press, 2016.

2fc256bd-66da-5cb4-b5ca-43283018a1db.name: Atabegs
2fc256bd-66da-5cb4-b5ca-43283018a1db.area: North Syria, north Mesopotamia [Iraq], southeastern Anatolia [Turkey]
2fc256bd-66da-5cb4-b5ca-43283018a1db.history:
*Atabeg*s or *atabey*s were high-level state officials entrusted with the education of the Great Seljuq princes. They also had authority in military and administrative matters.  
The atabegs took advantage of the contest for the throne among the sons of the Great Seljuq Sultan Melikşah \[Maliq Shah\] when he died in AH 485 / AD 1092 and proclaimed their independence. Among the most noteworthy atabeg states were the Atabegs of Damascus, the Zangids (Atabegs of Mosul), Ildenizids \[Eldigüzids or Ildegizids\], Salghurids and Atabegs of Erbil.  
The Atabegs of Damascus were also known as the Tuğtekinler \[Tughtiginids\] or Börids \[Burids\]. This dynasty was founded by Tuğtekin \[Tughtigin\], who was appointed as the atabeg for the son of Maliq Duqaq, son of Tutush who was the brother of Sultan Melikşah, in 497 / 1104, following the fall of the Seljuqs of Syria. They fell to Nur al-Din Mahmud, the Atabeg of Aleppo, in 548 / 1154.  
The Zangids are also known as the Atabegs of Mosul. This dynasty was founded by 'Imad al-Din Zangi, one of the commanders of the Great Seljuq Sultan Melikşah, in 520 / 1127 in Mosul. They fell in 619 / 1223 thanks to constant conflict with the Ayyubids.  
The dynasty of the Ildenizids, also known as the Atabegs of Azerbaijan, was founded in 535 / 1141 by Ildeniz as vassal to the Seljuqs of Iraq. They fell to the Khwarazm Shahs in 625 / 1228.  
The Salghurid Atabeg Dynasty was founded in 541 / 1147 by the Salghur branch of the Oghuz Turks, led by Atabeg Sunqur. They fell to the Mongolians in 682 / 1284.  
The Atabegs of Erbil were also known as Begtiginliler \[Begtiginids\] and their dynasty was founded in the mid 12th century by Zayn al-Din 'Ali Küçük bin Begtigin in southeastern Anatolia and northern Iraq. They came under Abbasid rule in 629 / 1232.

3a5bd0e8-5c73-5d1a-8242-521f5d28c002.name: Mudéjar period
3a5bd0e8-5c73-5d1a-8242-521f5d28c002.history:
Mudéjar art, the art of the Muslims who remained in the Iberian Peninsula after the Christian Reconquista (the Mudéjars), can be described as the integration of Islamic architectural and artistic forms with Christian art and crafts. Rather than a style *per se*, it is the expression of a trend towards Islamic forms. This 'mudéjarism' emerged as the Reconquista moved south and contact with the Islamic world became closer.  
The reason for this assimilation was the fascination the Muslim world exerted on the Christian aristocracy (and on Christian artists and artisans); the extraordinary luxury that Muslim rulers enjoyed was in complete contrast to the sober conditions in which Christian noblemen lived.  
The origins of this artistic association go back to the 12th century, but it was with the conquest of Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248) that it became widespread, culminating 150 years later with the conquest of Granada and an outpouring of 'mudéjarism' in civil and religious architecture. Alfonso XI and Pedro I of Castile (14th century), Pedro de Luna (Antipope Benedict XIII, late 14th–early 15th centuries), the Catholic Kings (15th century) and D. Manuel I of Portugal (late 15th–early 16th centuries) were the driving forces in this centuries-long process.  
Under the Christians, prestigious Mudéjar artists, occasionally organised into itinerant groups, worked for the élite, and the most exquisite Mudéjar pieces were exported en masse. Mudéjar artisans also formed renowned guilds of carpenters, bricklayers, saddlers and potters, among other trades.  
Political and aesthetic reasons were at the root of the decline of Mudéjar art in the 16th century. On one hand, the Counter-Reformation made all non-Christians undesirable (it was the time of the Inquisition and of the last expulsions of Muslims and Jews), and on the other, the models of the Italian Renaissance were beginning to appear. However, this did not prevent a popular Mudéjar style from surviving until the advent of Baroque.

3eb686ce-9607-530b-b1a3-688cf19fe53a.name: Zangids
3eb686ce-9607-530b-b1a3-688cf19fe53a.history:
The line of the Zangid Atabegs, also known as the Atabegs of Mosul, was founded in AH 521 / AD 1127 by Imameddin Zangi (‘Imad al-Din Zangi), a general of the Great Seljuq Sultan Melikşah I (Malik Shah) who governed Mosul (Iraq) and Syria. Mahmud, the Seljuq leader in Iraq, entrusted the education of his sons to Imameddin Zangi when Zangi became governor of Mosul in 521 / 1127. Zangi intended to found a great state. He first took Harran, Nusaybin and Aleppo, and further increased his power after invading Diyarbakır (Diyar Bakr) and Urfa (ancient Edessa). After the death of Imameddin Zangi in 541 / 1146, his son Seyfeddin Gazi (Sayf al-Din Ghazi) took over Mosul and his other son Nureddin (Nur al-Din), took charge of Syria.  
Nureddin Zangi wiped out the Fatimids in 567 / 1171 through his Ayyubid general Salah al-Din (Saladin) and extended his territory. He died in 569 / 1174. Seyfeddin Gazi, the governor of Mosul, died in 544 / 1148 and was succeeded by Kutbeddin Mevdud (Qutb al-Din Mawdud), who continued to reign until 565 / 1170.  
The disputes over succession that followed the deaths of Nureddin Zangi and Kutbeddin Mevdud, and the conflicts that arose with the Ayyubid dynasty founded by Salah al-Din in 569 / 1174, resulted in the decline of the Zangids and their eventual fall in 620 / 1223.  
The heyday of the Zangids was under Nureddin Zangi, governor of Syria. He had several castles in Syrian towns restored and built many mosques, caravanserais, *madrasas* (schools) and *imarets* (pious foundations). The Great Mosque of Mosul, the Nuriyya *madrasa*, Dar al-Hadith and the Maristan (hospital) of Damascus are some of the most important monuments from the period.

4ff94404-b748-5d95-93e3-648f784dd9ba.name: Qing
4ff94404-b748-5d95-93e3-648f784dd9ba.area: China, Taiwan, Tiber and Mongolia, as well as parts of central Asia
4ff94404-b748-5d95-93e3-648f784dd9ba.history:
The Qing dynasty was the last of the imperial dynasties of China. It was also the longest reigning dynasty, spanning the period from 1644 to 1912, and its rulers were renowned for their military prowess. The dynasty was also known as the Manchu dynasty as it was established by a Manchu clan (House of Aisin-Gioro), and half the royal officials were Manchu.  
  
The foundations of the Qing dynasty were laid when the Manchu people of northern China united against the Ming dynasty. Another group that went against the Ming dynasty was the Jurchen or the eastern barbarians. The group consisted of different tribes who inhabited the northeastern frontiers of the Ming empire. The Jurchen rose to power in the 1580s, led by a man named Nurhaci (also known as Nurgaci, 1559–1626), a Ming vassal who went on to unite all the Manchu clans. By 1583, after the death of his father and grandfather, Nurhaci emerged at 24 years old as the pre-eminent power in the region.  
  
Unlike the forebears of the Jurchen and other invaders and conquerors, Nurhaci’s tribesmen were not nomads. Their economy was dependent on agriculture, hunting and trade. In 1616, Nurhaci declared himself khan (“king”) of the Aisin dynasty. In a public document, he held the Ming rulers responsible for the deaths of his father and grandfather, calling them out for their abuse of power. The Ming dynasty responded by sending out a large number of militants against him, but this expeditionary force was defeated by a pan-Jurchen confederation led by Nurhaci.  
  
Nurhaci died in 1626, leaving his eighth son and heir, Hong Taiji (also known as Huang Taiji, 1626–43). Hong Taiji came to power as the descendent of his paternal grandfather, Giocangga. In 1616, Hong Taiji began driving out the Ming military from the Liaodong Peninsula. In 1629, he breached the Great Wall and occupied four Chinese cities: Luanzhou, Qian’an, Zunhua and Yongping. By 1636, he had established a functional government and went on to declare the formation of the “Great Qing” dynasty. Hong Taiji died on 21 September 1643, leaving behind a temporary power vacuum. After some negotiation it was decided that the emperor’s brother Dorgon (1612–50), together with the general named Jirgalang (1599–1655) would act as co-regents for Hong Taiji’s five-year-old son, Fulin. Fulin acceded to the throne in 1643 as the Shunzhi (“compliant rule”) emperor.  
  
From the 1750s to 1790s, the Qianlong emperor extended Qing control into the interior territories of Asia. At its height, the empire ruled over almost all of today’s mainland China, including Hainan, Taiwan, Mongolia, parts of Manchuria and northwest China. The Qing rulers maintained their Manchu custom and followed Tibetan Buddhism. The dynasty reached its peak in the 18th century but gradually deteriorated due to challenges from abroad, revolts within the kingdom, population growth, a disordered economy and corruption. The Qing dynasty was finally overthrown with the formation of the Republic of China in 1912.  
  
Bibliography  
• Smith, Richard J., The Qing Dynasty and Traditional Chinese Culture, Washington, DC: Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, 2015.

9edc1c13-a45a-5e4f-b590-717688101260.name: Abbasids
9edc1c13-a45a-5e4f-b590-717688101260.area: Ifriqiya [Tunisia], Jordan, Egypt, North Africa, Iraq
9edc1c13-a45a-5e4f-b590-717688101260.history:
The Abbasid era is considered to be the golden age of Islamic civilisation. The Abbasids were able to establish their supremacy by taking up the cause of non-Arabs who had been unjustly treated by the Umayyads and who, under the leadership of the rebel Abu Muslim al-Khurasani, successfully overthrew them in AH 132 / AD 750. The Abbasids became the caliphs of the Islamic empire that same year.  
The outer reaches of the empire were stabilised and consolidated by Caliph al-Mansur (AH 136–7 / AD 754–75) who broke up the monopoly of the Arabs over the political and economic institutions of the state and encouraged equality between the different groups that made up Abbasid society. Construction of the new capital, Baghdad, was completed in AH 138 / AD 766.  
The Abbasid period reached its zenith during the reign of Caliph Harun al-Rashid (AH 169–93 / AD 786–809) who achieved peace with Byzantium and exchanged embassies with Charlemagne of France. This period included the reigns of al-Ma'mun (AH 197–218 / AD 813–33), al-Mu'tasim (AH 218–27 / AD 833–42) and al-Wathiq (AH 227–32 / AD 842–7).  
The new wealth created by the switch from an agrarian to a trading economy reduced the social disparity between Arab and non-Arab communities and promoted the development of numerous craft industries, such as glass, ceramics and textiles, exported via the old trade routes from China to sub-Saharan Africa. Learning was encouraged and the key texts of Greek, Persian and Indian civilisations were translated into Arabic. Numerous great scholars furthered all fields of knowledge: philosophy (al-Kindi and al-Farabi), astronomy, mathematics (al-Khawarizmi), medicine (al-Razi and Ibn Sina), physics and chemistry (Ibn Sina), and their contributions would go on to influence the whole of medieval thinking.  
Abbasid power began to decline in the AH 5th / AD 11th century, and several provinces became independent. The Fatimids (AH 296–566 / AD 909–1171) established a rival caliphate in Egypt and Syria, and Tughrul (Tughril) Beg emerged from the Turkish regiments of the Abbasid army to take Baghdad in AH 447 / AD 1055. The final blow was dealt to the Abbasid Dynasty by the Mongols who swept through the Middle East and took Baghdad in AH 656 / AD 1258.

a999b9e1-b986-5792-8f1c-7764cd952822.name: Marinids and Wattasids
a999b9e1-b986-5792-8f1c-7764cd952822.area: Morocco and central Maghreb. Capital: Fez
a999b9e1-b986-5792-8f1c-7764cd952822.history:
After a century of brilliance, Almohad power was weakened by in-fighting before collapsing with the loss of control over the Sahara routes, the conquest of central Maghreb by the Hafsids of Tunisia and the progress of the *Reconquista* in Spain. Against this backdrop, Fez was taken by the Marinids (Banu Marin), Zenete nomads from Eastern Morocco. They strove to reunify the Maghreb for their own benefit (fall of Tunis, AH 747 / AD 1347). Abu Yusuf Ya'qub, the first Marinid sultan, went on to cross the Straits of Gibraltar several times, hindering the progress of the Christians and helping to save Granada.  
For the next 150 years, Morocco passed through a period of brilliance marked by artistic and cultural developments, the construction of numerous mosques and *madrasas* (schools) and the establishment of a new capital at Fez al-Jadid (674 / 1276).  
Following the heyday of the Marinids, an epidemic of the Black Death (748 / 1348) and the rebellions of Tlemcen and Tunis marked the decline of the dynasty, which failed to drive back the Spanish and the Portuguese.  
The Wattasids (Banu Wattas), a vizier family that succeeded the Marinids, declared themselves regents of the kingdom before taking power as sovereigns. However, the country sank into a grave economic crisis following the fall of Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, and the influx of refugees expelled from al-Andalus only served to increase popular frustrations and religious dispute.  
At the beginning of the 8th / 14th century, Morocco descended into anarchy and a cycle of conservatism and weakness. The Portuguese took Tangiers (875 / 1471) and occupied Safi, Azemmour, Mazagan and Agadir, while the Spanish established themselves in Mellilla.
a999b9e1-b986-5792-8f1c-7764cd952822.date_description_ah: The Marinids: AH 667–868 and the Wattasids: AH 869–955
a999b9e1-b986-5792-8f1c-7764cd952822.date_description_ad: The Marinids: AD 1269–1464 and the Wattasids: AD 1465–1549

ab22ae48-7fde-5229-a684-189558585904.name: Nasrids
ab22ae48-7fde-5229-a684-189558585904.history:
When the Almohad Caliph al-Ma'mun, enthroned in Seville in AH 624 / AD 1227, returned to Morocco, a member of the vizier Banu al-Ahmar family, Muhammad bin Yusuf bin Nasr, proclaimed himself king (627 / 1230) founding the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled Granada until 897 / 1492.  
He stayed in power by paying an annual tribute to the king of Castile and assisted passively in the breathtaking progress of the Christian Reconquista, with the surrender of Córdoba (633 / 1236), Jaen and Arjona (643 / 1246), and Seville (645 / 1248).  
Thanks to their plotting and dealing and the occasional military support of the Marinids, the Nasrids experienced a veritable golden age, the most stunning examples of which being the Alhambra and the Generalife. This splendour lasted until 886 / 1482 when Boabdil (Abu 'Abdallah) overthrew his father but failed to contain the Reconquista. Malaga fell in 892 / 1487; Baeza and Almeria in 894 / 1489, among other places. He ended up capitulating, and the Catholic kings entered Granada on 2 January 1492, closing the book on the epic that was 'al-Andalus'.  
The existence of al-Andalus as a Muslim political entity lasted nearly 800 years, but the Reconquista, which began in 722 (Battle of Pelayo / Covadonga) lasted nearly 900, continuing to 1610 with successive waves of expulsions of 'moriscos'.  
However, although al-Andalus ceased to exist as a political entity, its cultural and artistic influence lived on in Spain, where Mudejar art conditioned architectural thought until the 18th century, and in Morocco, where Hispano-Moorish architecture and craftsmanship successfully combined Hispano-Visigothic art with traits of the Muslim West and the Berbers, the latter having survived through the Sharif dynasties.

b372ff12-6d26-5b7b-84e0-c0679b12cfbb.name: Umayyads
b372ff12-6d26-5b7b-84e0-c0679b12cfbb.area: Syria, Asia Minor, Egypt, North Africa, Iraq, Iran, Central Asia, Iberian Peninsula
b372ff12-6d26-5b7b-84e0-c0679b12cfbb.history:
Founded in AH 41 / AD 661 by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan of the Bani Umayya family, the Umayyad dynasty was the first Islamic dynasty after the death of the Prophet Muhammad and the caliphs who succeeded him in 11 / 632. The most important Umayyad caliphs were Mu'awiya (41–60 / 661–80), 'Abd al-Malik (65–86 / 685–705) and Hisham (105–25 / 724–43). Under al-Walid I (86–96 / 705–15), military conquests reached as far as Spain and central Europe, while in the east the Umayyad kingdom extended to Transoxania and northern India. In 132 / 750, the Umayyad dynasty was overthrown by the Abbasids.  
During the Umayyad caliphate, many failed attacks were launched against Constantinople and the Byzantine Empire. In Spain, the Visigoths were defeated in 92 / 711, but the Muslim advance in central Europe was halted in 114 / 732 by Charles Martel at the Battle of Poitiers.  
The Umayyad dynasty introduced the idea of hereditary rulership in Islam and contributed many eminent figures to the caliphate from its family ranks.  
With the arrival of the Umayyads, the centre of political power in Islam shifted from Madina in the Arabian Peninsula to Syria, with Damascus becoming the new capital of the caliphate. This change had both political and cultural repercussions.  
Borrowing administrative practices from both the Byzantines and the Sassanids, the Umayyad caliphs became talented rulers, capable of controlling the first Islamic empire, which spread over a wide area thanks to its military successes.  
Social tensions quickly became apparent among non-Arab converts who, contrary to the teaching of Islam, did not enjoy the same rights as Arab Muslims. Rebellions in southern Jordan, Iraq and eastern Iran led to the gradual collapse of the dynasty.  
The Umayyads were energetic builders; their architects, artists and craftsmen were responsible for the towns, palaces, mosques and works of art that today symbolise the rich history of the early years of Islam.

b812e3d9-24d7-5ef1-bfc7-8031d0fa5144.name: Ayyubids
b812e3d9-24d7-5ef1-bfc7-8031d0fa5144.area: Egypt, Syria, southeastern Anatolia, Jazira, Yemen
b812e3d9-24d7-5ef1-bfc7-8031d0fa5144.history:
Events arising from the arrival in Baghdad of the leader of the Seljuq Turks in AH 446 / AD 1055 led to the Crusades and the invasion of Jerusalem in 492 / 1099. However, this did not prevent the Seljuqs from becoming the most powerful force in the Muslim world at that time.  
During the 5th / 11th century, faced with conflict with the Seljuq Turks and the Fatimids, the Seljuqs recruited *atabegs*, military commanders, as regional governors. In 468 / 1076, the Atabeg Atsiz, took Damascus from the Fatimids. In the 6th / 12th century, the powerful Zangid Dynasty reunified Syria. Nur al-Din, son of the founder of the Zangid dynasty, conquered Damascus in 548 / 1154, and his lieutenant Salah al-Din (Saladin) destroyed the Fatimid caliphate in 566 / 1171 and ended the Latin occupation of Jerusalem in 579 / 1187.  
The Atabegs and the Ayyubids introduced far-reaching changes to their realm, building numerous *madrasas* (schools) for the orthodox re-education of their subjects. With unprecedented levels of construction, the Seljuq period brought about a renaissance for Aleppo and Damascus, with the reconstruction of the Great Mosque and the foundation of the citadel in Damascus and the construction of mosques, *hammams* (baths), *madrasas*, *turbes* (mausoleums), *khanqahs* (hostels) and *ribats* (fortresses).  
The Zangid and Ayyubid princes managed to drive the crusaders from Edessa (Urfa) in 540 / 1146 and consolidated their hold on the region with the conquest of Egypt in 566 / 1171.  
In the middle of the 6th / 12th century, under Nur al-Din and his Ayyubid successors, Damascus again became a major centre of the Muslim world and prospered in all areas of society. As capital of an independent state, it came to assume all of the characteristics of a great city.  
From the 5th to the 7th centuries / 11th to the 13th centuries a number of factors favoured the development of art and urban activity. Artuqids, Zangids, Seljuqs of Rum and Ayyubids left their mark in various media, from pottery and metalwork to book arts and architecture. From the sober, classical forms of Ayyubid architecture to the brilliant decorative arts, this key period is characterised by high-quality artistic output, having the same importance for Syria as the Mamluk period for Egypt, or the Ottoman period for Turkey.

b866c59b-f81b-5655-972c-c4ac569b959e.name: Mughal
b866c59b-f81b-5655-972c-c4ac569b959e.history:
In Perso-Arab language the term Mughal means “the Mongol” or the “Mongolians”. Babur, the founder of the Mughal Dynasty who ruled from 1526 to 1530, was of Timurid–Mongolian heritage. On his paternal side he was a descendant of the warlord Amir Timur or Tamerlane, a fierce warrior of the late 14th and early 15th centuries, and on the maternal side of the family he was a descendant of Genghis Khan. Babur conquered a large territory extending from central Asia to the shores of the Mediterranean.  
  
By the late 15th century, the Mughals had begun patronizing the arts, commissioning the construction of imposing architecture and making grand illuminated manuscripts. They were considered refined and sophisticated. It was in 1526 at the battle of Panipat that Babur had a huge victory; he conquered northern India up to the Gangetic Plain after a struggle with Afghans, the Lodi Sultan of Delhi and the Rajputs under Rana Sanga of Mewar. In order to legitimise his rule, Babur went on to build three mosques.  
Babur died in 1530 and was succeeded by this son, Humayun, who inherited a territory that was yet to be consolidated. After being defeated by the Afghan chief of Bihar, Shir Shah Suri, Humayun was driven to the Persian court of the Iranian-Safavid court ruler, Shah Tahmasp I. With the help of the Persian emperor, he reconquered northern India in 1555. He died in 1556, in Delhi.  
  
Humayun’s son, Akbar, acceded to the throne at the young age of 12 years, and he went on to rule for nearly 50 years (1556–1605). Akbar is considered a very important ruler of the Mughal dynasty. Most significant were his many achievements; he set up an enduring foundation for Mughal governance, created inclusive policies and adopted an attitude of tolerance towards non-Muslims. This method of governing made him an amicable ruler and created a state that was syncretic in character.  
  
By the time Akbar passed away in 16o5, he had built a consolidated empire that would flourish under the rule of his son, Jahangir, and grandson, Shah Jahan. Jahangir followed the practices that Akbar had commenced during his reign. He had acceded to the throne in 1602 after clashing with his father and masterminding the death of Akbar’s close advisor, Abu al-Fazl, who he thought was against Jahangir becoming the heir. In 1611, he married a woman named Nur Jahan. She was a powerful, intelligent person who took the reins of the empire when Jahangir was ill.  
  
During its last phase, the Mughal empire was ruled by Nur Jahan and her family. One of these rulers was Prince Khurram, later known as Shah Jahan, a well-known military strategist. He was the one responsible for Jahangir’s victory during his reign. In 1614 he led a campaign against the Sisodiya Rajput fortress of Chittor and forced Rana Amar Singh to surrender. Jahangir was pleased with this victory and considered Khurram as heir apparent.  
  
Under Shah Jahan’s rule, the Mughal empire was prosperous, wealthy and internationally renowned. In the first 12 years of his reign, Shah Jahan pursued several military campaigns in a bid to subdue recalcitrant rulers. At the same time, he conquered territory in eastern India, Sind and the northwest. In 1636, he made a breakthrough in his campaign in order to increase territorial expansion into the Deccan. The Mughals signed a treaty with two dynasties of the Deccan, namely, Adil Shah of Bijapur and the Qutb Shahs of Golkonda. This resulted in 20 years of the Mughals’ peaceful coexistence with the Deccan Sultanates.  
  
In 1658, Shah Jahan’s son, Aurangzeb, ruled the Mughal empire from 1658 to 1707. He became the victorious leader after a battle of succession in which two of his brothers were killed, one brother was exiled to Burma and his father was imprisoned. His reign lasted for 49 years. He was known as Alamgir, the seizer of the world. His top achievement was to expand Mughal territory all the way to the Deccan. He subjugated the sultans of the Deccan and brought about a massive expansion of the empire.  
  
Aurangzeb has been considered an orthodox Muslim who broke away from the liberal traditions of his predecessors. Contrary to the image that has been painted, Aurangzeb was an Indian ruler who strove throughout his life to preserve and expand the Mughal empire, gain political power, and rule with his own vision of justice.  
  
The court of the Mughal successors was known for its aristocratic high culture. These rulers enjoyed entertainment in the form of music and poetry, commissioned miniature paintings and objects, and supported the construction of monumental architecture for the imperial Mughal court.  
  
From 1707 to 1857, however, the Mughal dynasty was in a period of decline. Aurangzeb’s death brought with it much turmoil due to courtiers vying with each other to gain power. Bahadur Shah I (1643–1712) attempted to alter the court’s religious policies and reform its administration. After his death in 1712, the empire was involved in feuds over who would be the next successor. He was ultimately succeeded by the 20th ruler of the Mughal dynasty, Bahadur Shah Zafar or Bahadur Shah II (1837–57). However, the last Mughal emperor had no power over the kingdom; rather, he was an emperor in title alone. Throughout the 18th century north India was at the mercy of indigenous and foreign power. The arrival of the East India Company marked the end of Mughal rule. By this time the Mughal empire existed in name only, while the East India Company governed the empire.

b93781fb-c7f0-5e7a-be03-24236c8c8b9d.name: Idrisids
b93781fb-c7f0-5e7a-be03-24236c8c8b9d.history: As in al-Andalus, the 'Alid leader Idris bin 'Abdallah, fleeing Abbasid repression, took refuge in Morocco and settled in Oualili (Roman Volubilis). He was proclaimed imam by the people before being assassinated by a spy sent by the Caliph Harun al-Rashid (AH 174 / AD 791). His son Idris II undertook to build a centralised state with its own capital (Fez), currency and army. His successors split and weakened the kingdom, although the spread of Islam throughout the country continued. The weakness of the Idrisids favoured foreign intervention, and Fez was taken first by the Fatimids of Ifriqiya, then by the Umayyads of al-Andalus.
